title.en: A spoon of sugar in the milk

text.en: The story goes that when the Parsis reached the coast of India, the local ruler sent them a full bowl of milk to say there was no room. A wise Parsi elder dissolved a spoon of sugar in the milk without letting a drop spill. The message: we will mix with you and sweeten your life without upsetting anything. This is one of many stories of people who came to India seeking safety and made it their home. In this chapter we meet some of them.

An old verse says, this is mine, that is not mine, so think the narrow-minded; for the generous the whole world is a family, vasudhaiva kutumbakam. India has often lived by this idea. Why did oppressed or persecuted people from other countries seek refuge here? Because India was a place where they could practise their faith and keep their identity without fear.
Jews came to India as traders and refugees over many centuries. India has proved to be a safe haven where they can practise their faith without fear. The Bene Israel lived on the Konkan coast just south of Mumbai. Although they lost their holy books they remembered their prayer, which says there is only one God. Over time they became part of Indian society while keeping their identity.
Zoroastrianism, one of the world's oldest religions, was founded by the prophet Zarathushtra in Central Asia. When Persia changed, a group of its followers sailed to India, bringing little more than their sacred fire and some hope for a safe home. They are known as Parsis, people from Persia, and they settled mainly in Gujarat and later in Mumbai. The legend of the wise man with milk and sugar shows how they promised to combine their ancient traditions with local culture. There are deep connections between Zoroastrian philosophy and India's ancient Vedic schools; Old Avestan, the language of the Avesta, and Vedic Sanskrit share many word roots and grammatical features. The Parsis contributed greatly to Indian life as industrialists, scientists, doctors and leaders, far beyond their small numbers.
Syrian Christians settled on the Kerala coast from very early times. They traded spices and other goods, married local women and formed new communities. A Syriac wedding ceremony today shows how old rites blend with local culture. Armenians from Persia gained patronage from the Mughal emperors in the 16th century and settled in Surat, Kolkata and Chennai. They built schools, churches and cemeteries and became influential in trade in silk, spices and precious stones. Armenian Christmas at the Armenian church in Kolkata shows how long their community has lasted. The Baha'i faith began in Persia in the mid-1800s with Baha'u'llah, and Baha'is began arriving in India in the late 19th century. Their Lotus Temple in New Delhi is one of the best-known buildings in the world.
The Siddis, people of African origin, came to India over centuries as traders, sailors and soldiers. They have a distinctive dance with African-style drumming. Hirabai Lobi, a Siddi social worker, was awarded the Padma Shri in 2023 for her service to her community.
In Warsaw, Poland, there is a Good Maharaja Square. During the Second World War, Maharaja Jam Sahib Digvijaysinhji of Nawanagar mobilised the Red Cross and other organisations to rescue Polish orphan children, took them to Jamnagar, and gave them a safe place to stay, food and care. India was a home away from home for them. After 1959 many Tibetans came to India with the Dalai Lama. Tibetan monasteries patterned on the originals were established in many places, especially in Karnataka, so that Tibetan Buddhists could follow their way of life without fear. The Tibetan medical system is practised at institutions such as the Men-Tsee-Khang in Dharamshala. In the 12th and 13th centuries the destruction of Nalanda and other Buddhist centres in eastern India also sent monks to Tibet, so India's and Tibet's links go back a long way.
These stories show a culture of acceptance and inclusion that is a part of the Indian ethos. This innate character of its people and culture has created a haven for the persecuted. Each community also enriched India with its food, art, trade and ideas.

problem.en: Explain the story of sugar in the milk.

text.en: The local ruler sent a full bowl of milk, meaning there was no room.
The wise man dissolved a spoon of sugar in it without spilling.
He meant the Parsis would fit in and enrich society.

prompt.en: List three communities who found a home in India and what they contributed.

requiredIdeas.en: Syrian Christians and Armenians: trade and institutions.
Tibetans and Siddis: culture, medicine and music.

commonMisconceptions.en: Thinking all communities came as invaders.
Thinking cultures must give up their identity to be accepted.

points.en: India has a long tradition of welcoming people seeking safety.
Jews, Parsis, Christians, Armenians, Baha'is, Siddis and Tibetans made homes here.
Each community kept its identity and enriched Indian life.
The Good Maharaja sheltered Polish children.
